content: Human placental lactogen (hPL), also known as human chorionic somatomammotropin (HCS), is a polypeptide hormone produced by the placenta. It is the human-specific form of placental lactogen and shares structural and functional similarities with human growth hormone. This hormone plays a critical role in modifying the maternal metabolic state during pregnancy to ensure an adequate energy supply for the developing fetus. Notably, hPL exhibits anti-insulin properties. hPL is secreted by the syncytiotrophoblast cells of the placenta during pregnancy. Its genetic encoding is located on chromosome 17q22-24, and the hormone was first identified in 1963. The molecular structure of hPL consists of a single polypeptide chain with 191 amino acid residues, linked by two disulfide bonds, and it contains eight helices. Its molecular mass is approximately 22,125 Daltons. hPL is exclusively present during pregnancy, with maternal serum levels increasing in proportion to the growth of the fetus and placenta. These levels peak near term, typically reaching 5–7 mg/L (5–7 micrograms/mL). Higher levels are observed in cases of multiple gestations. Only minimal amounts of hPL enter the fetal circulation, and its biological half-life is approximately 15 minutes. Physiologically, hPL influences the maternal metabolic system in several ways. It mimics the action of prolactin in bioassays, although its role in human lactation remains unclear. Metabolically, hPL reduces maternal insulin sensitivity, leading to elevated maternal blood glucose levels. This decrease in glucose utilization by the mother ensures an adequate supply of glucose for the fetus. In response, the maternal body compensates by increasing pancreatic beta-cell activity. Chronic maternal hypoglycemia can result in elevated hPL levels. Additionally, hPL promotes lipolysis, releasing free fatty acids that serve as an alternative energy source for the mother, thereby sparing glucose for fetal use. Ketones derived from these free fatty acids can cross the placenta and be utilized by the fetus. These metabolic adaptations are crucial for supporting fetal nutrition, even in cases of maternal malnutrition. hPL acts as a potent agonist of the prolactin receptor and a weak agonist of the growth hormone receptor. It binds to the prolactin receptor with an affinity comparable to that of prolactin, as demonstrated in studies using rabbit milk fat globule membranes. Both hPL and prolactin exhibit similar lactogenic activity in vitro, as shown in mouse and rat mammary gland explants. Furthermore, hPL has been found to stimulate DNA synthesis in human mammary fibroadenoma cells transplanted into mice, suggesting that it promotes mammary gland growth during pregnancy in a manner similar to prolactin. Given that hPL circulates at concentrations 100 times higher than prolactin during pregnancy, it is hypothesized to play a significant role in mammogenesis during this period. However, the relative affinities of hPL and prolactin for the human prolactin receptor have not been fully elucidated, and the effects of hPL on normal human mammary epithelial tissue remain unexplored. Consequently, the definitive role of hPL in human mammary gland development during pregnancy has yet to be established. hPL also exhibits weak growth hormone-like activity, promoting protein tissue formation in a manner similar to growth hormone. However, it is approximately 100 times less potent than growth hormone in this regard. Despite this, the blood concentration of hPL during pregnancy is more than 50 times higher than that of human growth hormone, indicating that its effects should not be disregarded. An enhancer element located 2 kilobases downstream of the hPL gene contributes to cell-specific control of its gene expression. Clinically, hPL has been used as an indicator of fetal well-being and growth. However, other fetal testing methods have proven to be more reliable. Additionally, normal pregnancies have been reported in cases where maternal hPL levels are undetectable.
